Good draft — it names the problem, population, and response, which is a solid foundation. Here's the rubric-mapped feedback, then a rewritten version.

---

## How the Draft Maps to the Rubric

The Need section is scored on **clarity of problem, target population, and data** (30% of total). Your draft handles clarity of problem reasonably well but is thin on the other two.

**What's working:**
- Clear problem framing (adult literacy gap → employment + family outcomes)
- Logical chain from cause to consequence
- Hints at local evidence (waitlists, library demand)

**What's missing:**
- No numbers anywhere — not a single statistic, rate, or count
- Target population is vague ("our neighborhood," "many adults") — no geography, demographics, or size
- "Waitlists are long" and "high demand" are asserted, not quantified or sourced
- No comparison to benchmarks (city, state, national) to show severity
- No trend data (is this getting worse?)
- No community voice (surveys, focus groups, participant quotes)
- No mention of gaps in existing services — why can't current providers meet this need?
- The link to children's outcomes is asserted but not evidenced

---

## Local Data Sources to Pull

**For adult literacy rates:**
- **PIAAC** (Program for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies) — national and state-level literacy/numeracy data from the National Center for Education Statistics
- **National Center for Education Statistics "Adult Literacy Estimates"** — county-level estimates of adults at or below Level 1 literacy
- **American Community Survey (ACS)** via census.gov — educational attainment, English proficiency, employment by census tract
- **State Department of Education / Adult Education Office** — enrollment and waitlist data for publicly funded adult literacy programs

**For employment and economic context:**
- **Bureau of Labor Statistics** local area unemployment statistics
- **County/city economic development reports**
- **Local Workforce Development Board** data on job seekers lacking credentials

**For family and child outcomes:**
- **School district data** — chronic absenteeism, kindergarten readiness, third-grade reading proficiency in schools serving your neighborhood
- **State report cards** for local schools
- Research linking parent literacy to child outcomes (e.g., National Institute for Literacy, ProLiteracy reports)

**For local demand:**
- Your own waitlist numbers (get exact counts and average wait times)
- Library system: ask for class registration, turn-aways, computer help requests
- Partner agencies: workforce centers, community colleges, family resource centers
- **Resident surveys or focus groups** — if you don't have these, even 15–20 brief interviews would strengthen the section

**For digital literacy:**
- **ACS data on household broadband and computer access** by tract
- **National Digital Inclusion Alliance** local reports if available

---

## Phrasing Hooks for the Rewrite

- "An estimated [X]% of adults in [specific geography] — roughly [N] residents — read at or below a basic level (PIAAC/NCES, [year])."
- "This rate is [X] times the statewide average of [Y]%."
- "In [neighborhood], [X]% of adults lack a high school credential, compared with [Y]% citywide (ACS [year])."
- "Our own intake data show [N] adults on the waitlist as of [date], with average waits of [X] months."
- "[Partner library] reports turning away [N] prospective learners in [year]."
- "In a [year] community survey (n=[X]), [Y]% of residents named adult education as a top-three priority."
- "Children of parents with low literacy are [X] times more likely to [outcome] ([source])."
- "Existing providers serve [N] adults annually citywide — meeting an estimated [X]% of need."

---

## Rewritten Statement of Need (~600 words)

Note: I've used **bracketed placeholders** everywhere real data should go. Do not submit without filling these in — reviewers will notice generic numbers and it will cost you points.

---

### Statement of Need

[Neighborhood], home to approximately [N] residents in [City], faces an adult literacy gap that constrains employment, family stability, and civic participation. According to the National Center for Education Statistics' county-level estimates ([year]), [X]% of adults in [County] — roughly [N] residents — read at or below Level 1, meaning they struggle with tasks as basic as comparing prices, following medication instructions, or completing a job application. In the census tracts [Organization] serves, this rate rises to an estimated [X]%, compared with a statewide average of [Y]% (PIAAC, [year]). American Community Survey data ([year]) show that [X]% of adults in these tracts lack a high school credential and [Y]% report limited English proficiency, more than double the citywide figure.

The consequences are concentrated and measurable. The [City] Workforce Development Board reports that [X]% of job seekers in [Neighborhood] lack the literacy or digital skills required for entry-level positions in the area's growing [sector] industry ([year]). Local unemployment in these tracts stands at [X]%, against [Y]% citywide (BLS, [month year]). Residents without foundational literacy are also [X] times more likely to live in households below the federal poverty line ([source]).

The impact extends to the next generation. Children whose parents read below a basic level are significantly more likely to enter kindergarten unprepared and to fall behind by third grade — a critical predictor of long-term school success ([source]). In [School District], third-grade reading proficiency in schools serving [Neighborhood] stands at [X]%, compared with [Y]% districtwide ([year] state report card). Chronic absenteeism in the same schools is [X] percentage points higher than the district average, a pattern research links in part to limited family capacity to support school engagement ([source]).

Residents themselves have named this gap as urgent. In a [year] community needs assessment conducted by [Organization/Partner] (n=[X]), [Y]% of respondents ranked adult education and job skills among the top three priorities for neighborhood investment. Focus group participants described being unable to help children with homework, navigate school portals, or apply for jobs online. One participant said: "[representative quote, 1 sentence]."

Existing services do not come close to meeting demand. Citywide, publicly funded adult literacy providers serve approximately [N] learners per year — an estimated [X]% of adults who need services ([source]). [Partner Library] reports [N] adults currently waitlisted for basic literacy and digital skills classes, with average waits of [X] months ([year] data). [Organization]'s own intake records show [N] adults turned away or deferred in the past [timeframe]. Current programs are also concentrated downtown, requiring a [X]-minute transit commute from [Neighborhood] — a barrier cited by [X]% of survey respondents who had considered enrolling.

Beyond capacity, a design gap persists: most available programs focus narrowly on reading instruction, without integrating the digital skills, workforce connections, and family-engagement supports that residents identify as essential. Adults in [Neighborhood] need coaching that meets them where they live and connects literacy gains to tangible goals — a job, a child's homework, a benefits application.

Without targeted, neighborhood-based programming, these adults will remain locked out of the labor market and their children will continue to enter school at a measurable disadvantage. The proposed program directly addresses this gap by delivering coaching in familiar community settings, integrating digital and workforce skills, and linking adult learning to family outcomes — a model matched to the specific barriers identified above.

---

## Quick Checklist Before You Finalize

- Replace every bracket with real data and cite the source + year
- Confirm your geography is consistent (neighborhood, tract, ZIP, council district — pick one and stick with it)
- If any statistic feels weak or missing, name it as a known limitation rather than fudging
- Add one real participant quote if you have IRB/consent, or an anonymized composite if you don't
- Keep the ratio roughly: 40% quantitative evidence, 30% consequences, 20% community voice, 10% service gap

Want me to move on to Target Population next, or pause here while you gather numbers?

## Verification Methods for Your Facts

**Neighborhood population (18,400):** Confirm against the most recent ACS 5-year estimate for tracts 12 and 13 combined. Cite "ACS 2020–2024 5-year estimates" or whichever vintage you're using. Easy to verify at data.census.gov.

**Low-literacy estimate (2,760):** This is your weakest number methodologically, because county-to-tract extrapolation assumes the tracts match the county average — but you're arguing they're higher-need. Two ways to strengthen:
- Pull the **NCES PIAAC Skills Map** directly; it provides tract-level or PUMA-level literacy estimates. This likely gives you a higher, tract-specific number that strengthens your case.

**Waitlist (142):** Get this in writing from the partner literacy center and library — a brief email or letter you can cite and attach. Specify the breakdown (e.g., "98 at [Center], 44 at [Library]") if available.

**Broadband (1,820 households):** Confirm the ACS table (likely S2801 or B28002) and the vintage. Also note what share of total households this represents — 1,820 out of how many? That percentage is more legible to reviewers.

**Screening tools:** Confirm your staff is certified or trained to administer TABE or CASAS, and mention this briefly — it signals rigor.

**Additional data worth pulling for these tracts:**
- Median household income and poverty rate (ACS)
- Educational attainment (% without HS diploma, % without any college)
- Race/ethnicity and primary language spoken at home
- Share of households with children under 18
- Unemployment and labor force participation

---

## How This Maps to the Rubric

Program Design & Activities is worth **30%** and is scored on **logic, timeline, and staffing**. Reviewers want to see a clear theory of change, activities tied to the need, an evidence base, and a feasible operational plan.

**What's working:**
- Three distinct activity streams (1:1 coaching, small groups, digital labs)
- Individualized learning plans tied to validated assessments
- Explicit cohort structure with intake, mid-point, exit
- Named partners with implied roles
- Staffing model gestured at (local coaches + program manager)

**What's missing or thin:**
- No logic model — activities aren't explicitly tied back to the needs in Section 2
- No evidence base — why one-on-one coaching? Why 12 weeks? Why this dosage?
- No participant pathway — what does a learner's journey actually look like, week by week?
- Partner roles are vague — "for referrals" doesn't tell reviewers what each partner contributes
- No mention of retention strategy (adult ed attrition is notoriously high; reviewers know this)
- No cultural/linguistic responsiveness, despite the earlier note about English learners
- Missing dosage specifics (hours per week, total contact hours)
- No fidelity/quality assurance detail beyond "program manager oversees"
- Family-engagement and workforce modules named but not described
- Two "community sites" unnamed — reviewers will wonder about accessibility, cost, hours

---

## Partner Roles — Suggested Specifics

Rather than listing partners generically, assign each a concrete function. Reviewers love MOUs (and often require them as attachments).

- **Branch library:** Co-location of digital skills labs; access to devices and Wi-Fi; shared promotion; referrals from library staff trained in warm hand-offs
- **Workforce center:** Direct referral pipeline both ways; co-delivery of the workforce navigation module; access to job placement services and labor market information
- **Two elementary schools:** Referrals from family liaisons and teachers; co-hosted family literacy nights; data-sharing agreement (with consent) on children's attendance and reading outcomes to measure two-generation impact
- **Consider adding:** A community college for bridge-to-credential pathways; a faith or civic organization for outreach; a health or benefits-navigation partner for wraparound referrals

---

## Evidence Base to Cite

The strongest grant narratives anchor each activity in research. Sources you can draw from:

- **ProLiteracy** — research briefs on adult literacy program design and outcomes
- **National Research Council** report *Improving Adult Literacy Instruction* (2012)
- **What Works Clearinghouse** (Adult Education topic area) — evidence-based practices
- **COABE** (Coalition on Adult Basic Education) — practitioner research
- **OCTAE** (Office of Career, Technical, and Adult Education) — federal evidence reviews
- **Two-generation approaches:** Ascend at the Aspen Institute; Annie E. Casey Foundation reports on dual-generation strategies
- **Digital literacy:** National Digital Inclusion Alliance; EveryoneOn
- **Workforce integration:** research on **Integrated Education and Training (IET)** models, which pair literacy with workforce skills and show stronger outcomes than literacy-only approaches

---

## Phrasing Hooks

- "The program's design is grounded in a two-generation theory of change: when parents gain literacy, digital, and workforce skills, both their economic trajectory and their children's school outcomes improve ([source])."
- "Each learner will receive [X] contact hours over 12 weeks, exceeding the [Y]-hour threshold associated with measurable literacy gains (NRS/[source])."
- "Coaching is paired with workforce navigation and family engagement — an Integrated Education and Training approach shown to produce [X] greater gains than stand-alone literacy instruction ([source])."
- "Retention — a central challenge in adult education — will be addressed through [specific strategies]."
- "Fidelity will be monitored through [observation, coach supervision, data review cadence]."

---

## Rewritten Program Design & Activities (~800 words)

---

### Program Design & Activities

**Theory of Change.** The program is built on a two-generation theory of change: when adults in tracts 12 and 13 gain foundational literacy, digital, and workforce skills in a setting that integrates learning with real-life goals, they move toward stable employment and are better equipped to support their children's school success. This dual focus responds directly to the needs identified above — a 15% low-literacy rate, a 142-person waitlist, 1,820 households without broadband, and third-grade reading proficiency in local schools well below the district average. Each program component is designed to address one or more of these specific barriers.

**Design Rationale.** The approach draws on two bodies of evidence. First, **Integrated Education and Training (IET)** models — which pair basic skills instruction with workforce and digital content — have been shown to produce stronger literacy and employment outcomes than stand-alone literacy classes (OCTAE; What Works Clearinghouse). Second, **two-generation approaches** that explicitly link adult learning with family and child engagement are associated with improvements in both adult economic mobility and children's school readiness (Ascend at the Aspen Institute). Our model combines these frameworks with the neighborhood-based delivery residents identified as essential in the [year] community survey.

**Core Activities.** The program delivers three integrated activity streams across two co-located community sites — the [Branch] Library and [Elementary School] family resource room — selected for walkability, evening availability, and existing resident trust.

*One-on-one coaching* (minimum 2 hours/week per learner) pairs each participant with a trained coach who develops and iterates an Individualized Learning Plan (ILP) grounded in the learner's TABE or CASAS results, employment goals, and family priorities. Coaches use evidence-based adult literacy curricula (e.g., [curriculum]) and adjust pacing based on biweekly progress checks.

*Small-group workshops* (2 hours/week, cohorts of 10–12) build peer support and cover shared content: workforce navigation (résumés, online applications, interview skills, labor market information), family engagement (navigating school portals, supporting children's reading at home, parent–teacher communication), and life skills (benefits access, financial basics, health literacy).

*Digital skills labs* (2 hours/week) are held in the library computer lab and address the broadband and device gap directly. Content progresses from device fundamentals through online job search, email, school communication platforms, and telehealth access. Participants without home broadband receive referrals to the [City] Affordable Connectivity program and, where available, loaner hotspots.

Total dosage per learner is approximately **72 contact hours** over 12 weeks — above the 60-hour threshold associated with measurable NRS-level literacy gains.

**Participant Pathway.** Each learner moves through four phases: (1) *Intake and assessment* (week 0): eligibility verification, TABE or CASAS administration by certified staff, goal-setting, and ILP development. (2) *Active learning* (weeks 1–11): coaching, workshops, and labs, with a mid-point check-in at week 6 to recalibrate goals. (3) *Exit assessment and transition planning* (week 12): post-assessment, outcome documentation, and warm hand-off to next steps (employment, further education, or continued coaching). (4) *Follow-up* (months 3 and 6 post-exit): check-ins to document employment, enrollment, and family-engagement outcomes.

**Cadence.** Four 12-week cohorts per year, each enrolling 50 learners (200 total annually). Cohorts are staggered to maintain continuous intake and to accommodate residents whose schedules shift with seasonal work.

**Partners and Roles.** The **[Branch] Library** co-hosts the digital skills lab and provides device and Wi-Fi access, trained referral staff, and shared promotion. The **[City] Workforce Center** supplies a bidirectional referral pipeline, co-delivers the workforce navigation module, and provides direct access to job placement services. **[Elementary School A and B]** refer parents through family liaisons, co-host quarterly family literacy nights, and — with parent consent — share anonymized data on children's attendance and third-grade reading proficiency to support two-generation outcome measurement. MOUs with each partner are attached.

**Staffing.** The program is delivered by **four part-time Literacy Coaches** (0.5 FTE each) hired from within the neighborhood where possible, each with adult education experience and trained in TABE/CASAS administration, trauma-informed instruction, and culturally responsive practice. A **full-time Program Manager** oversees curriculum fidelity, coach supervision, partner coordination, and data quality. A **0.25 FTE Data and Evaluation Specialist** manages the learner data system and evaluation activities. Bilingual (Spanish/English) capacity is built into coach hiring to serve the [X]% of residents who are English language learners.

**Retention and Quality Assurance.** Recognizing that adult education attrition typically exceeds 40%, the program incorporates evidence-based retention strategies: on-site childcare during sessions, transit stipends, cohort-based peer support, flexible make-up sessions, and proactive outreach after missed sessions. Fidelity is monitored through monthly coach observations by the Program Manager, biweekly case conferencing, and quarterly data reviews against benchmarks established with the evaluator.

---

## Quick Notes Before You Finalize

- Confirm the actual curriculum you'll use and name it specifically — reviewers often look for named evidence-based materials
- The "72 contact hours" and "above 60-hour threshold" framing is strong; verify the specific NRS guidance language your state uses
- If you don't yet have signed MOUs, say "MOUs in development" rather than implying they're done — reviewers may ask
- The two-generation data-sharing piece is powerful but legally sensitive; confirm with the school district what's actually feasible under FERPA before promising it
- If childcare and transit stipends aren't in the budget, add them — they're mentioned here and reviewers will cross-check against Section 8
- Consider whether four 0.5 FTE coaches is realistic for 50-learner cohorts; the math is roughly one coach per 12–13 learners per cohort, which is tight if coaching is truly 1:1

Ready for Staffing & Implementation Timeline, or do you want to pause and gather MOUs / confirm curriculum first?

## Staffing Structure — Suggested Clarifications

A simple reporting line to show in the narrative or an org chart attachment:

- **Executive Director** (existing, in-kind) supervises the **Program Manager**
- **Program Manager** supervises **four Literacy Coaches** and the **Data & Evaluation Specialist**

Also worth naming in the staffing table or narrative:

## Timeline — Expanded Milestones to Fold In

A credible 12-month timeline usually includes these workstreams in parallel, not just sequentially:

**Workstream 1 — Staffing:** job posting (M0), interviews (M1), onboarding (M2), initial training (M2), ongoing supervision (M3+), annual performance review (M12)

**Workstream 2 — Partnerships:** MOU finalization (M0–M1), referral workflow design (M1–M2), partner staff orientation (M2), joint events scheduled (M3+)

**Workstream 3 — Systems and Site Setup:** data system configuration (M0–M2), curriculum procurement (M1), site preparation at library and school (M1–M2), device/materials procurement (M1–M2)

**Workstream 4 — Recruitment and Intake:** outreach materials developed (M1–M2), community outreach begins (M2), Cohort 1 intake (M2–M3), rolling recruitment thereafter

**Workstream 5 — Program Delivery:** Cohort 1 (M3–M5), Cohort 2 (M6–M8), Cohort 3 (M9–M11), Cohort 4 (M12–M14 — crosses into year 2)

**Workstream 6 — Evaluation and Reporting:** baseline data collection (M3), mid-point review (M6), interim funder report (M6), annual evaluation (M12)

Note the cohort math: four 12-week cohorts = 48 weeks of active instruction. With two weeks between cohorts for intake/exit, you need about 56 weeks — slightly more than a calendar year. Either run cohorts in parallel (two coaches each), or accept that the fourth cohort crosses into year 2. Flag this explicitly so reviewers don't catch it as a gap.

## Phrasing Hooks

- "The program will be delivered by a team of [N] staff totaling [X] FTE, supervised by a full-time Program Manager with [Y+] years of adult education leadership experience."
- "Hiring prioritizes residents of tracts 12 and 13, consistent with the program's community-based approach; at least two of the four Literacy Coaches will be bilingual (Spanish/English) to serve the [X]% of residents who are English language learners."
- "A two-week pre-service training in Month 2 ensures all staff begin Cohort 1 fully prepared across pedagogy, assessment, trauma-informed practice, and curriculum."
- "Fidelity is sustained through monthly 1:1 supervision, biweekly case conferencing, and quarterly structured observations using a [tool/rubric]."
- "The timeline includes contingency: if hiring is delayed, Cohort 1 start shifts to Month 4, with no reduction in annual enrollment achieved by [mitigation]."

## Rewritten Staffing & Implementation Timeline (~400 words)

---

### Staffing & Implementation Timeline

**Staffing Structure.** The program will be delivered by a team totaling **3.25 FTE**, supervised by the Executive Director (0.05 FTE, in-kind) who provides organizational oversight and board liaison. Direct program leadership is provided by a full-time **Program Manager** responsible for hiring, partner coordination, curriculum fidelity, data quality, and reporting. The Program Manager supervises **four part-time Literacy Coaches** (0.5 FTE each) and a part-time **Data and Evaluation Specialist** (0.25 FTE). Existing [Organization] finance and operations staff provide back-office support in-kind. A full staffing table and org chart are attached.

**Qualifications.** The Program Manager will hold a minimum of a bachelor's degree with [5+] years of adult education or workforce program leadership, including supervisory experience. Literacy Coaches will have prior adult education or tutoring experience and, within 30 days of hire, complete certification in TABE and CASAS administration. Hiring prioritizes residents of tracts 12 and 13 and candidates with lived experience in the neighborhood; **at least two of the four coaches will be bilingual (Spanish/English)** to serve the [X]% of residents who are English language learners. The Data and Evaluation Specialist will bring experience with adult education data systems (e.g., LACES, state NRS reporting) and basic analysis.

**Implementation Timeline (Year 1).**

| Month | Milestones |
|---|---|
| **M0** | Program Manager starts; Data Specialist onboarded; coach job postings live; MOU finalization with library, workforce center, schools; data system configuration begins |
| **M1** | Coach interviews; curriculum and materials procured; site preparation at library and school; outreach materials developed |
| **M2** | Coaches onboarded; two-week pre-service training (adult ed pedagogy, trauma-informed care, TABE/CASAS, curriculum, cultural responsiveness); partner staff orientation; Cohort 1 recruitment and intake |
| **M3** | **Cohort 1 begins** (50 learners); baseline data entered; monthly coach supervision begins |
| **M4–M5** | Cohort 1 mid-point assessments (M4); Cohort 1 completion and exit assessments (M5); first quarterly fidelity observations |
| **M6** | **Cohort 2 begins**; interim funder report submitted; mid-year evaluation review |
| **M7–M8** | Cohort 2 delivery; first family literacy night co-hosted with partner schools |
| **M9** | **Cohort 3 begins**; 3-month follow-up with Cohort 1 participants |
| **M10–M11** | Cohort 3 delivery; annual coach performance reviews |
| **M12** | **Cohort 4 begins** (completes in M14); year-end evaluation; annual report to funder |

**Fidelity and Supervision.** The Program Manager conducts **monthly 1:1 supervision** with each coach, **biweekly case conferencing** across the team, and **quarterly structured observations** using a program-specific fidelity rubric. The Data Specialist runs **monthly data quality reviews** with the Program Manager.

**Contingency.** If coach hiring extends beyond Month 2, Cohort 1 shifts to Month 4 and subsequent cohorts compress by two weeks; annual enrollment of 200 is preserved. In the event of mid-cohort coach turnover, remaining coaches absorb caseloads with temporary support from a pre-identified pool of qualified substitute tutors maintained through our partnership with [community college / volunteer corps].

## Quick Notes Before You Finalize

- The fourth cohort finishes in Month 14 — this is honest and common in grant timelines, but if the funder expects all activity within 12 months, you'll need to either run cohorts in parallel or reduce to three cohorts of ~67 learners each. Flag this in a sponsor conversation if possible.
- 3.25 FTE across four coaches + PM + data = roughly 50 learners per coach per year across cohorts; cross-check this matches the 1:1 coaching dosage you promised in Section 4 (2 hrs/week × 12 learners × 12 weeks ≈ 288 hours per cohort per coach, which is feasible at 0.5 FTE but tight)
- Confirm the Executive Director in-kind FTE is also reflected in Section 9 (Organizational Capacity) and the budget
- If MOUs aren't yet signed, say "MOU finalization" rather than "MOUs in place" — reviewers cross-check
- The contingency paragraph is a quiet strength; many applications omit it, and including it signals operational maturity

Good draft — you've got the right mix of output and outcome measures. Here's the mapping, gaps, and rewrite.

---

## How This Maps to the Rubric

Outcomes & Evaluation is worth **20%** and is scored on **measurable outcomes, methods, and baseline**. This section (Outcomes & Objectives) handles the "what we're measuring and at what level" piece; Section 7 (Evaluation Plan) handles the "how we measure it" piece. Keep that division clean — don't repeat.

**What's working:**
- A mix of reach (200/year), learning (literacy level gain), economic (employment), engagement (retention), and family (parent engagement) outcomes — this breadth maps well to the two-generation theory of change
- Explicit baseline collection and follow-up cadence
- Retention target is included, which many applicants forget

**What's missing or thin:**
- **No distinction between outputs and outcomes.** "200 adults served" is an output; reviewers want this separated from participant-level outcomes.
- **Baselines are TBD or implicit.** Reviewers want to see either an existing baseline or a concrete plan to establish one — not "TBD."
- **Some targets need sanity-checking against the field:**
  - 60% gaining a level is ambitious; national NRS data typically show 40–50% for comparable programs
  - 75% retention is aggressive for adult ed, where 50–60% is more typical even with strong supports
  - 40% employment at 6 months is reasonable but needs a defined denominator (job-seeking at intake)
- **No measurement tools named** for employment, parent engagement, or retention
- **No definition of "increased engagement"** — reviewers will ask: compared to what, measured how
- **No disaggregation plan** — reviewers increasingly want to see outcomes broken out by subgroup (English learners, parents, etc.)
- **No mention of children's outcomes** despite the two-generation framing in Section 4 — this is a missed opportunity

---

## Suggested Target Adjustments

I'd suggest tempering a couple of these to protect your credibility with reviewers who know the field, and to protect yourself from under-performing on your own stated targets.

- **Literacy level gain:** 50% is defensible and well-supported by NRS benchmarks; 60% is reach-level. Consider "50% gain at least one NRS level, with a stretch goal of 60%" or just go with 50%.
- **Retention:** 65% attending ≥75% of sessions is a strong but defensible target for adult ed with wraparound supports. 75% is possible but uncommon.
- **Employment:** 40% is reasonable if the denominator is clearly "job-seeking at intake." Make that explicit.
- **Parent engagement:** 50% reporting increased engagement is reasonable if the measure is self-report. If you want to cite school-side data (attendance, portal logins), lower the target and sharpen the measure.

Reviewers generally prefer **conservative, defensible targets with evidence-based rationale** over aspirational numbers without grounding.

---

## Measurement Tools to Name

- **Literacy gain:** TABE 11/12 or CASAS GOALS pre/post, aligned to NRS Educational Functioning Levels
- **Digital skills:** Northstar Digital Literacy Assessment (widely used, free, aligned to adult ed)
- **Employment:** self-report at 3- and 6-month follow-up, verified where possible through partner workforce center data-share
- **Retention:** attendance logs from the learner data system (LACES or equivalent)
- **Parent engagement:** a validated instrument like the Family Engagement Survey (Harvard Family Research Project) or a program-adapted version with pre/post administration; supplement with school-reported data where consent allows
- **Participant satisfaction:** short exit survey (consider Net Promoter Score or similar)
- **Children's outcomes (if two-generation data-sharing goes through):** school-reported attendance and third-grade reading proficiency, with parent consent

---

## Phrasing Hooks

- "Outputs measure what the program delivers; outcomes measure what changes for participants."
- "By the end of Year [X], [N] adults will have [outcome], measured by [tool], compared with a baseline of [Y] established at intake."
- "Target reflects NRS benchmarks for comparable Integrated Education and Training programs ([source])."
- "Outcomes will be disaggregated by English language learner status, parent/caregiver status, and employment status at intake."
- "Among job-seeking participants (defined at intake as [criteria]), [X]% will obtain employment within 6 months of program exit."

---

## Rewritten Outcomes & Objectives (~400 words)

---

### Outcomes & Objectives

The program's outcomes are organized by the two-generation theory of change: direct learner outcomes (literacy, digital, employment), engagement outcomes (retention, satisfaction), and family-level outcomes (parent engagement and, where data-sharing allows, children's school indicators). All targets are grounded in National Reporting System (NRS) benchmarks for comparable Integrated Education and Training programs and tempered by the realities of adult education in high-barrier neighborhoods.

**Outputs (Services Delivered).**

- **200 adults enrolled annually** (600 over 3 years), with at least 90% drawn from census tracts 12 and 13.
- **Four 12-week cohorts delivered** per year across two community sites.
- **At least 72 contact hours** offered per participant (coaching, workshops, digital labs).
- **Quarterly family literacy nights** co-hosted with partner schools (4 per year).

**Participant Outcomes (What Changes for Learners).**

*Learning outcomes.* **50% of participants will gain at least one NRS Educational Functioning Level** between intake and exit, measured by pre/post TABE 11/12 or CASAS GOALS administered by certified staff. This target reflects NRS benchmarks for comparable programs and will be treated as a floor; a stretch goal of 60% applies to participants completing full dosage (≥75% attendance). **70% of digital lab participants will advance at least one level on the Northstar Digital Literacy Assessment** between intake and exit.

*Economic outcomes.* Among participants identified at intake as **job-seeking** (defined as unemployed or underemployed and actively seeking work), **40% will obtain employment within 6 months of program exit**, measured through self-report at 3- and 6-month follow-up and verified where possible through data-sharing with the [City] Workforce Center.

*Engagement outcomes.* **65% of enrolled participants will complete the program**, defined as attending at least 75% of scheduled sessions through week 12. Attendance is tracked in the learner data system. **85% of completing participants will report satisfaction** with the program on an exit survey.

*Family outcomes.* Among participants who are parents or caregivers of school-age children, **50% will report increased engagement with their child's school**, measured by pre/post administration of the Family Engagement Survey (adapted from Harvard Family Research Project) and defined as improvement of at least one scale point on the composite engagement measure. Where parent consent and district data-sharing agreements allow, we will also track **children's school attendance and third-grade reading proficiency** as supplementary two-generation indicators.

**Baselines.** Baselines for all participant-level outcomes will be established at intake (week 0) using the measurement tools named above. Program-level baselines for retention and satisfaction will be established during Cohort 1 and used to calibrate targets for Cohorts 2–4.

**Disaggregation.** All outcomes will be disaggregated by English language learner status, parent/caregiver status, and employment status at intake, to identify differential impact and inform program adjustments.

---

## Quick Notes Before You Finalize

- If your state uses specific NRS reporting language (EFL gain, MSG — Measurable Skill Gain), align your terminology exactly; funders aligned with WIOA will look for this
- The "stretch goal of 60%" framing protects you if you don't hit it but signals ambition
- Confirm the parent engagement survey you'll actually use; if you're adapting one, name the adaptation process briefly
- The children's outcomes line is powerful but contingent on FERPA-compliant data-sharing — if that MOU is uncertain, soften to "we will explore data-sharing with partner schools"
- Make sure the Evaluation Plan (Section 7) doesn't repeat these targets but instead explains the *methods*: design, data flow, analysis, QA, reporting, use of findings
